State management in React is one of those things everyone has an opinion about and nobody agrees on, so I stopped forming my own opinion entirely. For about a year, any time I needed state — local, global, some context provider, a reducer, whatever — I’d describe the behavior I wanted and let AI pick the approach and write it. Sometimes useState, sometimes context, sometimes a small custom hook, sometimes a full reducer pattern, whatever it decided fit the situation.
The app worked, mostly, the whole year. Then a bug showed up where a piece of UI would very occasionally show stale data for a second after a save, and tracking it down took me four days, because the state for that one feature was actually spread across three different mechanisms that had all been generated independently and never designed to agree with each other about who owned the truth.
Why this felt fine for a long time
Each piece of state management, in isolation, was a reasonable choice given what I’d described. Local component state for something that clearly only mattered to one component. Context for something a few components needed. A reducer for something with more complex transitions. AI was making sensible calls case by case, and each…
